newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK MARCH STATE EXPENDITURES IN LINE WITH FORECASTS - MIN.
newsitem.headline: GREEK MARCH STATE EXPENDITURES IN LINE WITH FORECASTS - MIN.

text.p: Greek Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis told a news conference on Thursday that government expenditures were in line with projections in March.
"Government expenditures have been kept within the forecast range. Revenues seem to be going well but will be finalised after the end of this month," said Christodoulakis.
Interest expenditures were lower than projected and this was the result of more systematic, faster interest rate cuts than anticipated, he added.
The finance ministry has asked other ministries to submit their budgets quarterly in order to detect discrepancies with annual budgets and minimise them, said Christodoulakis.
The ministry will push forward a presidential decree to set up state corporations in charge of procurements.
"These companies will charge as expense money spent on technology, machinery and equipment. But, at the same time they will enter it as an asset," said Christodoulakis.
He added that this practice has been used extensively in France and helps avoid the deterioration in the fiscal picture of a country whenever money is spent for technological advancement.
Also, progress has been made for the establishment of a double-entry T-account system for hospitals, universities, municipalities and insurance organisations, he said.
Christodoulakis said the ministry had been able to draw a yield curve for three-month to seven-year government debt paper.

"In the long-end, the curve is downward because the market expects better fiscal performance in the future. In the short-term, it is upward, because one-year T-bills offer higher yields after the impact of a long period of heavy short-term borrowing seems to be subdued," he said.

On April 1, the Greek finance ministry will issue two-year zero coupon notes at an unchanged gross yield of 10.1 percent and 12-month T-bills at a gross rate of 10.3 percent, down 20 basis points from the previous issue.
Christodoulakis said he expected the auction to be successful because the rates were good.
Standard & Poor's has affirmed the Hellenic Republic's BBB-minus long-term foreign currency rating and revised the foreign currency rating outlook to positive from stable, on Wednesday.
He added that the S&P ratings will also have a positive effect on the auction next Tuesday. --Margarita Sotiropoulou, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
